claims.text: The baseline MnNiSi-based material exhibits a strong magnetocaloric response.
The baseline MnNiSi-based material suffers from brittle mechanical behavior during thermal cycling.
Approximately 3 at.% Co can be substituted for Ni in the MnNiSi-based alloy through controlled alloying and homogenization.
Substituting Co for Ni will produce grain refinement and a more uniform grain-size distribution.
Co substitution will increase solid-solution strengthening.
Co substitution will improve grain-boundary cohesion and reduce brittle intergranular features.
Co has a magnetic moment similar to that of Ni.
The similarity of the Co and Ni magnetic moments means that Co substitution will not significantly alter the magnetostructural transition.
The large magnetocaloric effect in the material is derived from an intrinsic magnetostructural transition.
Co incorporation causes slight lattice distortion.
Co-induced lattice distortion enhances dislocation mobility.
Co-induced lattice distortion increases grain-boundary strength.
The proposed microstructural changes will improve ductility and fracture toughness.
Relative to the Co-free baseline, the 3 at.% Co alloy will exhibit enhanced ductility and fatigue resistance.
The 3 at.% Co alloy will retain a magnetocaloric-effect magnitude within approximately 10% of the Co-free baseline.
The hypothesis should hold near the magnetocaloric transition, within approximately ±20 K, under comparable applied-field changes.
The hypothesis should hold for similarly arc-melted and homogenized alloys containing up to about 3 at.% Co.
Co additions above approximately 3 at.% may perturb the balance between the magnetic and structural transitions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes solid-solution strengthening while also claiming that solute-induced lattice distortion enhances dislocation mobility. Conventional solid-solution strengthening generally operates by impeding dislocation motion, so the stated dislocation mechanism is internally in tension with the proposed strengthening mediator.
